Vulnerable @xhmikosr/decompress or decompress package present (CVE-2026-53486) AIWeaponization High
Inventory hunt that surfaces hosts carrying a decompress version affected by CVE-2026-53486 (@xhmikosr/decompress < 10.2.1, >= 11.0.0 < 11.1.3, or unmaintained decompress <= 4.2.1). These hosts can be pushed a crafted archive that writes/reads files outside the extraction directory, so they are the exposure baseline for the runtime detections below. Rationale: Keys off the exact CVE id CVE-2026-53486 from the advisory; TVM already tracks the fixed versions (10.2.1 / 11.1.3) so this is a clean deploy-blast-radius hunt rather than a behavioural one. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mp2f-45pm-3cg9 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/decompress/CVE-2026-53486/ • https://vulert.com/vuln-db/CVE-2026-53486
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Package present but pinned behind a build stage that never extracts untrusted archives (dev-only devDependency)
  • Transitive copy already deduped to a fixed version at runtime while the tree still lists the vulnerable range
  • Container image layer cached with the old version but overridden at runtime
  • Air-gapped host that only ever extracts internally-produced archives
  • SBOM lists the package but the code path is dead / behind a disabled feature flag
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): confirm the resolved runtime version (npm ls @xhmikosr/decompress / decompress) — a lockfile range is not the installed version. Step 2 (contain): for any host that extracts network-sourced archives, bump to @xhmikosr/decompress 11.1.3 (or 10.2.1) and, as interim mitigation, run extraction as a non-root user. Step 3 (hunt): pivot to the runtime UCs below on the same DeviceName to check whether an escape has already been attempted (symlink/hardlink creation, writes to /etc/cron.d, /etc/ld.so.preload, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys).

Node archive-extraction process writing to Linux persistence paths (decompress dir-escape) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts a Node.js process (the runtime that hosts the vulnerable decompress library) creating or modifying files under canonical persistence locations — cron drop-dirs, systemd unit dirs, sudoers.d, and SSH authorized_keys. CVE-2026-53486 lets a crafted archive escape the extraction root and land an entry anywhere the process can write; these directories are the highest-value landing zones and none are ever a legitimate output target for archive extraction. Rationale: Article states a crafted entry can be written 'outside that directory'; a node process (the decompress host) writing into cron/systemd/sudoers/authorized_keys is never a legitimate extraction target, so the destination path itself is the escape signal. Persistence paths are the MITRE-canonical landing zones for a write-anywhere primitive, not verbatim advisory strings — flagged as hunting for that reason. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mp2f-45pm-3cg9 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qgfr-5hqp-vrw9
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1098.004 T1543.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node-based config-management/IaC agent (e.g. a homegrown deployer) that legitimately writes systemd units
  • Node process management tools like pm2 generating a systemd unit via 'pm2 startup'
  • A CI runner written in Node that provisions cron jobs as part of a build
  • Cloud-init or provisioning scripts that shell out to node to template a sudoers.d fragment
  • Developer tooling that writes ~/.ssh/authorized_keys during a workstation bootstrap
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "pm2" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("startup","deploy")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine and parent chain — a legitimate extraction targets an app/tmp dir, not /etc; confirm whether an archive was fetched over the network moments before (correlate FileCreated of a .tar/.zip in a temp dir by the same node PID). Step 2 (contain): quarantine/rollback the written file (cron/unit/authorized_keys), kill the node process, and revoke any SSH key added. Step 3 (hunt): sweep the host for the symlink/hardlink escape UC and for setuid/ld.so.preload writes; check for outbound C2 from any cron/systemd payload just dropped.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs")
| where (FolderPath has_any ("/etc/cron.d","/etc/cron.hourly","/etc/cron.daily","/etc/cron.weekly","/etc/systemd/system","/usr/lib/systemd/system","/etc/sudoers.d")
        or (FileName =~ "authorized_keys" and FolderPath has "/.ssh"))
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("dpkg","apt","apt-get","rpm","yum","dnf","cloud-init","ansible")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","nodejs")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/cron.d","/etc/cron.hourly","/etc/cron.daily","/etc/cron.weekly","/etc/systemd/system","/usr/lib/systemd/system","/etc/sudoers.d","/.ssh/authorized_keys")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, DvcAction, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node extraction writing ld.so.preload or setuid/privileged path as root (CVE-2026-53486 privesc) AIInstallation High
Alerts when a Node.js process running as root writes /etc/ld.so.preload or drops into privileged binary dirs (/usr/local/sbin, /usr/local/bin) during archive extraction. CVE-2026-53486 applies file modes with 'mode & ~umask', preserving setuid/setgid bits, and lets entries escape the output dir — so a root-context extraction can plant a preloaded library or a setuid binary for privilege escalation. This is near-zero in normal operation. Rationale: Anchored to the advisory's mode-bit finding ('File modes were applied as mode & ~umask ... does not remove the setuid, setgid, or sticky bits ... matters when extraction runs as root'). ld.so.preload and setuid drops into /usr/local/s?bin are the canonical root-write privesc targets for that primitive; keyed on InitiatingProcessAccountName==root to keep FP near zero. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mp2f-45pm-3cg9 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/decompress/CVE-2026-53486/
ATT&CKT1548.001 T1574.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A root-run Node build tool legitimately installing a native addon into /usr/local/bin
  • node-gyp / install scripts placing compiled helpers under /usr/local during a package build
  • In-house deployment tooling written in Node that manages ld.so.conf.d for custom libs
  • Container entrypoint (running as root) that node-templates a binary into /usr/local/bin
  • Monitoring/APM agent installers shelling through node to drop a preload shim
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "node-gyp" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("install","rebuild","prebuild")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): inspect the written file — dump /etc/ld.so.preload contents or stat the /usr/local binary for setuid/setgid bits; confirm no legitimate root-run build (node-gyp, npm install of a native module) explains it. Step 2 (contain): isolate the host, remove the preload entry / setuid binary, and rotate any credentials reachable from root on that box; if in a container, kill and rebuild from a patched image (decompress >= 11.1.3). Step 3 (hunt): review process executions immediately after the write for any binary that loaded the preloaded library or ran with elevated tokens, and check the same host for the symlink-escape and persistence-path UCs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName =~ "root"
| where FolderPath has "/etc/ld.so.preload" or FileName =~ "ld.so.preload"
      or FolderPath has_any ("/usr/local/sbin","/usr/local/bin","/etc/ld.so.conf.d")
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("dpkg","apt","apt-get","rpm","yum","dnf","make","cloud-init")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","nodejs")
| where ActorUsername =~ "root"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/ld.so.preload","/etc/ld.so.conf.d","/usr/local/sbin/","/usr/local/bin/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, DvcAction, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cilium Envoy admin socket abuse: TLS secret / config disclosure via admin.sock (CVE-2026-49445) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a local process on a Kubernetes node reading sensitive Envoy admin endpoints (/certs, /config_dump, /clusters) over the world-accessible Cilium Envoy admin.sock. Only cilium-agent/cilium-envoy should ever touch this socket, so any curl/wget/socat/python/nc process referencing it plus a read endpoint is anomalous and indicates exploitation of the mode-0777 socket. Rationale: Anchored on the concrete artifacts corroboration surfaced: the world-accessible socket is admin.sock (mode fixed to 0660 in PR #44512) and the article's 'Exposing TLS secrets' maps precisely to Envoy's /certs and /config_dump admin endpoints (Envoy admin docs). Excluding cilium-* binaries makes non-cilium access to this socket high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/44512 • https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/operations/admin.html • https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/security/network/proxy/envoy/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1005 T1613
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cilium/Isovalent support engineer running `cilium-sysdump` or manual curl against admin.sock during troubleshooting
  • Custom Prometheus exporter or monitoring wrapper script scraping /stats or /config_dump for observability
  • Platform team debugging L7 policy by dumping Envoy config on a node
  • CI/e2e test harness that exercises the admin interface
  • SRE gathering diagnostics via a non-cilium helper script that shells out to curl
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cilium-sysdump", "cilium-dbg", "cilium-health", "cilium-bugtool"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the acting process, its parent, and the user/UID. Confirm it is NOT cilium-agent/cilium-envoy and not a sanctioned sysdump/monitoring job. Capture which endpoint was hit — /certs and /config_dump mean TLS material and full mesh config may be disclosed. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the node, rotate any TLS secrets/SDS certs served by Envoy on that node, and confirm Cilium is upgraded to a patched build (v1.17.14 / v1.18.8 / v1.19.2) so admin.sock is mode 0660. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same host/UID for other admin.sock access, for destructive endpoint hits (/quitquitquit, /drain_listeners), for lateral movement from the identity, and search other nodes for the same process ancestry.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "admin.sock"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/certs", "config_dump", "/clusters", "server_info", "/stats", "/listeners", "/runtime")
| where FileName !in~ ("cilium-agent", "cilium-envoy", "cilium")
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cilium-agent", "cilium-envoy"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256

ImProcessCreate

| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "admin.sock"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/certs", "config_dump", "/clusters", "server_info", "/stats", "/listeners", "/runtime")
| where ActingProcessName !has "cilium"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine !has "cilium-agent" and ActingProcessCommandLine !has "cilium-envoy"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cilium Envoy admin socket abuse: destructive DoS via /quitquitquit /drain_listeners (CVE-2026-49445) AIActions on Objectives High
Alerts when a local process invokes disruptive Envoy admin operations over the world-accessible Cilium admin.sock — /quitquitquit (terminate Envoy), /drain_listeners, /healthcheck/fail, /reset_counters. These directly implement the article's 'disrupting traffic' and 'terminating the Envoy process' impacts and have no legitimate manual use against the Cilium-managed Envoy. Rationale: The article explicitly lists 'Disrupting traffic in the cluster' and 'Terminating the Envoy process' as impacts; Envoy admin docs confirm /quitquitquit terminates the process and /drain_listeners + /healthcheck/fail disrupt serving. These are irreversible operational actions no legitimate operator issues against the Cilium-managed Envoy, making this alertable at high confidence. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/44512 • https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/operations/admin.html • https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/security/network/proxy/envoy/
ATT&CKT1489 T1499
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator manually draining a node for maintenance who scripts /drain_listeners against the Cilium Envoy instead of using the node-drain workflow
  • Chaos-engineering / resilience test intentionally failing Envoy healthchecks
  • Support engineer restarting a wedged Envoy via /quitquitquit during an incident
  • Custom automation that resets Envoy stat counters via /reset_counters before a benchmark
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cilium-sysdump", "cilium-dbg", "cilium-bugtool"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Correlate the process/user/UID with any approved change or maintenance window; check whether Envoy on the node restarted or dropped L7 traffic immediately after (cilium-agent logs, pod readiness flaps). 2) CONTAIN: Cordon/isolate the node, restore Envoy (cilium-agent will respawn it) and verify L7 policy enforcement resumed, then ensure the cluster is upgraded to a patched Cilium (v1.17.14 / v1.18.8 / v1.19.2). 3) HUNT: Look for prior read abuse of the same admin.sock (/certs, /config_dump) from the same identity, repeated destructive calls across multiple nodes (coordinated DoS), and the initial access vector that placed the attacker on the node.

| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("quitquitquit", "drain_listeners", "healthcheck/fail", "reset_counters")

| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cilium-agent", "cilium-envoy"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

2026-07-06 4 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Rocket.Chat anonymous Livechat visitor bootstrap chained to file-upload access · [LLM] Rocket.Chat file-upload request carrying Livechat auth params (IDOR signature) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children

Rocket.Chat Livechat file-upload ID enumeration sweep (ObjectId harvest) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts an unauthenticated source pulling many distinct /file-upload/{fileId} objects while carrying the Livechat authorization params (rc_room_type=l + rc_token) — the continuous ObjectId-prediction harvest described in the Aikido disclosure. High volume of distinct fileIds from one IP via the Livechat auth path is the signature of the mass file-capture exploit. Rationale: Anchors on the exact exploit request shape from the article's Python PoC — GET /file-upload/{fileId} with rc_room_type=l and rc_token query params — combined with a distinct-fileId volume threshold that captures the 'retrieve all generated valid IDs continuously' harvest. Legit Livechat file access does not fan out across dozens of unrelated fileIds. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/predicting-mongodb-objectid-rocket-chat • https://hackerone.com/reports/3687142 • https://docs.rocket.chat/docs/rocketchat-security-fixes-updates-and-advisories • https://github.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/releases/tag/8.5.0
ATT&CKT1213 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuinely busy Livechat helpdesk session where a visitor downloads many attachments the agent sent (all belonging to that room)
  • Load balancer / uptime monitor health-checking a file-upload URL repeatedly (usually one fixed path, not distinct fileIds)
  • Internal backup or migration tooling iterating over uploads with a service token
  • Authorized DAST/vulnerability scanner (Aikido, Burp) replaying the PoC against a staging instance
  • CDN origin prefetch pulling attachments
Suppression filter
| where UserAgents !has_any ("kube-probe","ELB-HealthChecker","UptimeRobot","Pingdom")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the source IP's full request timeline; confirm the requests carry rc_room_type=l + rc_token and hit many DISTINCT fileIds, and check whether the Rocket.Chat build predates 8.5.1/8.4.4/8.3.6/8.2.6/8.1.6/8.0.7/7.13.9/7.10.13 (vulnerable). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/reverse proxy, and if patch is not yet deployed, disable Livechat (Admin > Omnichannel) or upgrade immediately. 3) Hunt: enumerate which fileIds returned HTTP 200 to that IP to scope leaked files, and search for the same IP creating anonymous visitors (POST /api/v1/livechat/visitor) to identify the session token used.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where Url has "/file-upload/" and (Url has "rc_room_type=l" or Url has "rc_token=")
| extend FileId = extract(@"/file-upload/([^/?]+)", 1, Url)
| where isnotempty(FileId)
| summarize DistinctFiles = dcount(FileId), Requests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), UserAgents = make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, 5), Statuses = make_set(HttpStatusCode, 10) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname
| where DistinctFiles >= 25   // >=25 distinct file-upload IDs fetched via the Livechat auth path from one source in 1h = ObjectId harvest sweep
| order by DistinctFiles desc

Rocket.Chat anonymous Livechat visitor bootstrap chained to file-upload access AIExploitation Medium
Detects the full unauthenticated exploit chain: a single source registering an anonymous Livechat visitor (POST /api/v1/livechat/visitor), requesting a room (GET /api/v1/livechat/room), then reading files via /file-upload/ within a short window. This is the session-bootstrap primitive the exploit uses to mint a valid rc_token/rc_rid before harvesting arbitrary files. Rationale: Chains the three exact endpoints from the PoC (POST /api/v1/livechat/visitor, GET /api/v1/livechat/room, GET /file-upload/) within a 10-minute window keyed on source IP — the minimum footprint of the unauthenticated access-control bypass. Individually noisy, together it is the exploit workflow. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/predicting-mongodb-objectid-rocket-chat • https://hackerone.com/reports/3687142 • https://github.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/releases/tag/8.5.0
ATT&CKT1190 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A real anonymous helpdesk visitor who opens Livechat and then downloads a file the agent shared (legitimate, same room)
  • Synthetic monitoring that scripts a Livechat conversation end-to-end
  • Support-widget embedded on a high-traffic page generating many short-lived visitor sessions
  • Rocket.Chat mobile/desktop client polling room + upload endpoints during normal use
  • Pen-test / bug-bounty researcher reproducing the chain on an authorized instance
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the visitor registration and file reads share one SrcIpAddr and that the /file-upload/ requests carry rc_room_type=l; verify the instance version against the patched list. 2) Contain: block the IP at the proxy/WAF and, if unpatched, disable Livechat or upgrade to the fixed build. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP to the enumeration-sweep detection to measure how many files were pulled, and review Content-Disposition/response sizes to identify sensitive filenames leaked.
ImWebSession

Rocket.Chat file-upload request carrying Livechat auth params (IDOR signature) AIExploitation Medium
Single-event signature for the Rocket.Chat access-control bypass: a GET to /file-upload/ whose query string carries rc_room_type=l together with rc_token — the Livechat authorization path being used to read a file, exactly as in the disclosed exploit. Surfaces individual exploit attempts even below the harvest threshold. Rationale: Uses the verbatim exploit primitive from the PoC — /file-upload/ path plus rc_room_type=l and rc_token query params — as an atomic, Sigma-portable signature. It matches even a single probe, complementing the volume- and chain-based UCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/predicting-mongodb-objectid-rocket-chat • https://hackerone.com/reports/3687142
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Livechat visitor downloading an attachment shared in their own helpdesk room (identical request shape)
  • Rocket.Chat client appending rc_room_type/rc_token to file URLs during normal Livechat file rendering
  • WAF or SSL-inspection proxy replaying the request as part of active response testing
  • Authorized researcher/DAST scan on a staging instance
  • URL-preview/link-unfurl bot following a Livechat file link
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the response status — HTTP 200 means a file was served; note the SrcIpAddr, Content-Disposition filename, and whether the source ever authenticated. 2) Contain: if the instance is unpatched (pre 8.5.1/8.4.4/8.3.6/8.2.6/8.1.6/8.0.7/7.13.9/7.10.13), upgrade or disable Livechat and block the IP. 3) Hunt: aggregate this IP's requests to see if it escalates into the distinct-fileId harvest sweep, and correlate with anonymous visitor registrations from the same address.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where HttpMethod =~ "GET"
| where Url has "/file-upload/" and Url has "rc_room_type=l" and Url has "rc_token="
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Twig SSTI markers in request-controlled fields against Craft/Formie public forms AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP requests carrying Twig template syntax ({{ }}, {% %}) in the User-Agent, Referer, or query string reaching a Craft CMS site running Formie. CVE-2026-52889 copies these request-derived Hidden-field defaults straight into Craft's Twig render layer, so Twig markers in these fields are the earliest observable of exploitation of a public form. Rationale: Uses the exact request-derived input surface named in the advisory (User Agent, Referer, Current URL, Query Parameter) and Twig delimiters {{ / {% (plus URL-encoded %7b%7b). Web-request telemetry only exists in Sentinel W3CIISLog / Splunk Web DM; Defender AH, Datadog standard sources, Falcon FDR and CloudWatch do not carry HTTP request headers, so those queries are intentionally empty. Cross-checked against the sibling Formie SSTI advisory CVE-2026-45697 and the Craft SSTI advisory GHSA-94rc-cqvm-m4pw. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-565m-g33j-jq96 • https://dailycve.com/craft-cms-formie-plugin-twig-injection-via-hidden-field-cve-2026-45697-critical/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94rc-cqvm-m4pw
ATT&CKT1190 T1221
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Web vulnerability scanners (Burp, Nuclei, Acunetix) sending {{7*7}} SSTI probes
  • Client-side JS frameworks (AngularJS/Vue/Mustache) passing {{ }} template strings in query params
  • Marketing/analytics referrers containing mustache placeholders like {{campaign}}
  • Bug-bounty researchers testing the public form
  • URLs carrying JSON blobs with doubled braces
Suppression filter
| where scStatus == 200 and csUriStem !contains "/api/" and csUserAgent !has_any ("AngularJS","Vue")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the source IP in the window; confirm the target csUriStem is a page that renders a Formie form and whether scStatus==200 (server processed the payload vs 404/403). Decode the payload from UA/query/cookie. 2) Contain: if the payload contains RCE gadgets or scStatus 200 on a form page, block the source IP at the WAF and confirm Formie is on 3.1.27+; if not, apply the workaround (remove request-derived Hidden-field defaults) immediately. 3) Hunt: pivot to endpoint telemetry on the web host for php/w3wp spawning shells (UC3) and review the same source IP for gadget strings (UC2).
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem !endswith ".js" and csUriStem !endswith ".css" and csUriStem !endswith ".png" and csUriStem !endswith ".woff2"
| where csUriQuery contains "%7b%7b" or csUriQuery contains "{{" or csUriQuery contains "%7b%25" or csUriQuery contains "{%"
     or csUserAgent contains "{{" or csUserAgent contains "{%" or csUserAgent contains "_self.env"
     or csReferer contains "{{" or csReferer contains "{%"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, csReferer, scStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Active Twig RCE gadget strings in Craft/Formie HTTP request inputs AIExploitation High
High-fidelity detection for Twig-to-PHP RCE gadgets (_self.env.registerUndefinedFilterCallback / getFilter / craft.app) delivered via the request-controlled Hidden-field defaults exploited by CVE-2026-52889. Unlike generic {{ }} probing, these tokens are unambiguous command-execution attempts. Rationale: Anchors on the documented Twig RCE gadget chain _self.env.registerUndefinedFilterCallback + getFilter and Craft's exposed craft.app object — these strings virtually never appear in benign traffic, so this warrants alerting. Web-request headers/query are only available in Sentinel/Splunk web logs; Defender/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch do not carry them. Gadget syntax corroborated via PayloadsAllTheThings PHP SSTI and the Craft SSTI advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-565m-g33j-jq96 • https://swisskyrepo.github.io/PayloadsAllTheThings/Server%20Side%20Template%20Injection/PHP/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94rc-cqvm-m4pw
ATT&CKT1190 T1221 T1059
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized pentest/red-team validating CVE-2026-52889 post-patch
  • Vulnerability scanner with a Twig-specific SSTI plugin
  • WAF that replays blocked payloads into a downstream access log
  • Security-training or CTF traffic against a staging Craft instance
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ("<authorized_scanner_ip_placeholder_removed>") and csUserAgent !has_any ("Nuclei","nuclei","Burp")
Response runbook
1) Triage: decode the full payload from csUriQuery/csUserAgent/csReferer, identify the command inside getFilter()/filter('system'), and check scStatus + the response size for signs the command executed. Confirm the source IP is not an authorized scanner. 2) Contain: block the source IP, take the affected web node out of the pool if RCE is likely, and force-upgrade Formie to 3.1.27+ (or remove request-derived Hidden-field defaults). 3) Hunt: on the web host, run UC3 for php/w3wp child shells, review new files in web roots (webshell drop) and outbound connections from the PHP worker, and search all web logs for the same source IP and gadget tokens over a wider window.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriQuery has_any ("registerUndefinedFilterCallback","registerUndefinedFunctionCallback","getFilter","_self.env","craft.app")
     or csUserAgent has_any ("registerUndefinedFilterCallback","registerUndefinedFunctionCallback","getFilter","_self.env","craft.app")
     or csReferer has_any ("registerUndefinedFilterCallback","getFilter","_self.env")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, csReferer, scStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Craft/PHP/IIS web worker spawning a command shell (Formie SSTI RCE outcome) AIExploitation High
Detects the PHP FastCGI, php-fpm, or IIS worker process backing a Craft CMS site spawning a command interpreter or recon LOLBin — the post-exploitation footprint of a successful Twig SSTI RCE via CVE-2026-52889. A web worker launching cmd/powershell/sh is not normal Craft behaviour. Rationale: Anchors on the specific web-tier parents of a Craft/PHP deployment (php-cgi.exe, php-fpm, w3wp.exe backing IIS+FastCGI, nginx/httpd) spawning shells/recon LOLBins — the concrete execution outcome of the Twig system()/exec gadget the advisory warns can lead to RCE. Purely endpoint telemetry, so no web-log or CloudWatch query. Not covered by generic Office-spawn-script or encoded-PS rules. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-565m-g33j-jq96 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94rc-cqvm-m4pw
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin running Craft console commands (php craft resave/queue/run) that legitimately shell out
  • Image-processing plugins (ImageMagick/GD) invoked by php calling system utilities
  • Deployment/build steps (composer, npm) executed under the web-service account
  • Monitoring/backup agents launched by the web worker
  • Scheduled Craft queue jobs spawning curl for outbound webhooks
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "craft" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("queue/run","resave","gc","migrate")) and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine and the parent InitiatingProcessCommandLine — a shell running whoami/id/net/certutil under the web-service account with no interactive admin session is high-signal; correlate the timestamp with UC1/UC2 web-log hits from the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the web host, kill the child process, and revoke/rotate any credentials accessible to the web-service account; confirm Formie is patched to 3.1.27+. 3) Hunt: enumerate files written by the php/w3wp worker (webshells), outbound connections from the worker process, new local accounts or scheduled tasks, and repeat the process-tree hunt across all other Craft/Formie web nodes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-cgi.exe","php.exe","php-fpm","w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

Apache Camel: KeycloakSecurityPolicy has Improper Authentication, Missing Authentication for Critical Function and Failing Open Vulnerabilities

CVEsCVE-2026-53913

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Vulnerable camel-keycloak version exposed (CVE-2026-53913 affected range) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Forged unsigned (alg:none) JWT Bearer token reaching Apache Camel route (CVE-2026-53913)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Forged unsigned (alg:none) JWT Bearer token reaching Apache Camel route (CVE-2026-53913) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP requests whose Authorization: Bearer value is an unsigned/forged JWT — a header decoding to {"alg":"none"} or a token with an empty signature segment — which the vulnerable camel-keycloak KeycloakSecurityPolicy accepts without verification in its default (empty requiredRoles/requiredPermissions) config. A forged token that returns HTTP 2xx indicates a successful unauthenticated bypass into server-side route work, up to unauthenticated RCE where the route forwards to a code-execution producer. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete forged-token shape: an unsigned JWT carries a {"alg":"none"} header whose base64url form starts eyJhbGciOiJub25l (alg-first) / eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJub25l (typ-first), and an unsigned JWT has an empty third (signature) segment — both are effectively never produced by a legitimate Keycloak-issued token. Corroborated by IONIX and basefortify write-ups confirming the alg:none/forged-JWT bypass shape. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ionix.io/threat-center/cve-2026-53913/ • https://basefortify.eu/cve_reports/2026/07/cve-2026-53913.html • https://www.tenable.com/plugins/nessus/299985
ATT&CKT1190 T1606
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners / pen-test tools (Burp, Nuclei CVE-2026-53913 template, OWASP ZAP) deliberately sending alg:none tokens during an authorized assessment
  • Internal API compatibility tests that intentionally send malformed bearer tokens to validate rejection behaviour
  • A custom identity provider that legitimately issues unsigned tokens over a trusted internal channel (rare, misconfiguration)
  • Copy-paste/truncated tokens in a client bug that drop the signature segment, producing a trailing-dot token
Suppression filter
| where HttpStatusCode >= 200 and HttpStatusCode < 400  // keep only requests the failing-open policy actually let through
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.0.0.0")  // add authorized scanner source IPs here
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the matching requests and check HttpStatusCode — a 2xx/3xx on a route behind KeycloakSecurityPolicy means the bypass succeeded; base64url-decode the Token header to confirm alg:none. Identify the target Camel route and what producer it forwards to (file, exec, http, sql). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, and apply the vendor mitigation now — set a non-empty requiredRoles/requiredPermissions on every KeycloakSecurityPolicy (forces the verification path), set allowTokenFromHeader=false where not needed, or add upstream token validation; plan upgrade to camel-keycloak 4.18.3 / 4.21.0. 3) Hunt: review all requests from the same src IP/UA for follow-on actions on the reached route (command execution, file writes, data reads) and pivot to server process/file telemetry on the Camel host for that time window.
// Requires WAF / API-gateway / reverse-proxy logs that capture the Authorization header into ASIM ImWebSession
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| extend AuthHdr = tostring(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| where AuthHdr startswith "Bearer " or AuthHdr startswith "bearer "
| extend Token = trim(" ", substring(AuthHdr, 7))
// forged unsigned JWT: base64url of {"alg":"none"...} (alg-first or typ-first), or a JWT with an empty signature segment
| where Token has_any ("eyJhbGciOiJub25l", "eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJub25l")
    or Token matches regex @"^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]+\.$"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, Token
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable camel-keycloak version exposed (CVE-2026-53913 affected range) AIReconnaissance High
Inventories hosts running Apache Camel camel-keycloak in the vulnerable ranges (>=4.15.0 <4.18.3 and >=4.19.0 <4.21.0) so the SOC can prioritise patching and apply the KeycloakSecurityPolicy mitigation before the auth bypass is exploited. This is an exposure/attack-surface pivot rather than an in-progress-attack detection. Rationale: Directly keys on the article's CVE id (CVE-2026-53913) and the concrete affected package (org.apache.camel:camel-keycloak) and fixed versions 4.18.3 / 4.21.0. Software-inventory match is deterministic, hence high confidence and low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ionix.io/threat-center/cve-2026-53913/ • https://securityonline.info/apache-camel-patches-critical-keycloak-leveldb-flaws/

Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion falls in >=4.15.0 <4.18.3 or >=4.19.0 <4.21.0, and determine whether the host is internet-facing and whether any route actually uses KeycloakSecurityPolicy with the default empty requiredRoles/requiredPermissions. 2) Contain: for exposed vulnerable hosts, apply the interim mitigation immediately (non-empty requiredRoles/requiredPermissions, allowTokenFromHeader=false, or upstream token validation) and schedule upgrade to 4.18.3 / 4.21.0. 3) Hunt: on each confirmed-vulnerable host, run the forged-alg:none-JWT web-log detection over the last 30 days to check for prior exploitation, and review the Camel route configs for producers capable of code execution.

Apache Camel DNS SSRF: inbound HTTP request carrying dns.server / dns.name control headers AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to a Camel platform-http endpoint that smuggle the raw dns.server, dns.name, dns.domain, dns.type or dns.class parameters (CVE-2026-48205). Because these names lack the Camel/camel prefix, HttpHeaderFilterStrategy lets them pass from the HTTP boundary into the Exchange, letting an unauthenticated client repoint the DNS resolver or resolve arbitrary internal hostnames. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact vulnerable parameter names (dns.server / dns.name / dns.domain / dns.type / dns.class) which are the raw pre-fix header/param constants — the migration guidance renames them to CamelDns*, so any surviving dns.* on the HTTP boundary is either an attacker or a pre-upgrade misconfig. Camel platform-http binds both query params and headers into the Exchange, so query-string capture in web logs is a valid vector. Cross-checked GHSA-hcm8-x79p-wx2w and Akamai's Camel header-smuggling write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hcm8-x79p-wx2w • https://www.akamai.com/blog/security-research/march-apache-camel-vulnerability-detections-and-mitigations • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-48205
ATT&CKT1190 T1071.004
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Burp/Nuclei) probing the Camel endpoint with dns.* payloads
  • Internal QA/dev traffic still using legacy dns.* header names before completing the CamelDns* migration
  • A legitimately-designed DNS-lookup API that intentionally exposes a dns.name / dns.domain query parameter
  • Synthetic monitoring/health-check tooling replaying old request templates
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has "Nessus" and RequestClientApplication !has "Nuclei" and RequestClientApplication !has "Burp" | where SourceIP !startswith "10." and SourceIP !startswith "192.168."
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SourceIP is external/untrusted and check the HTTP response status — a 200 with the app reaching the camel-dns producer indicates successful exploitation; note the dns.server value (attacker resolver) and any dns.name/dns.domain values (internal hosts probed). 2) Contain: add a WAF rule to strip/deny dns.server, dns.name, dns.domain, dns.type, dns.class and term on ingress, and prioritise upgrading Camel to 4.14.8 / 4.18.3 / 4.21.0. 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound DNS from the app host (UC2) to spot the SSRF egress, and search the same logs for other prefix-less Camel header smuggling and for internal hostnames enumerated via dns.name/dns.domain.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has_any ("dns.server","dns.name","dns.domain","dns.type","dns.class")
    or RequestContext has_any ("dns.server","dns.name","dns.domain","dns.type","dns.class")
    or Message has_any ("dns.server","dns.name","dns.domain","dns.type","dns.class")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestContext, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Apache Camel DNS SSRF via dns.* HTTP request parameters (CVE-2026-48205)

description: Detects inbound HTTP requests carrying the raw dns.server/dns.name/dns.domain/dns.type/dns.class parameters that bypass Camel HttpHeaderFilterStrategy and drive the camel-dns producer (SSRF via DNS).

      - 'dns.server='
      - 'dns.name='

  condition: selection
level: medium
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where (Web.uri_query="*dns.server=*" OR Web.uri_query="*dns.name=*" OR Web.uri_query="*dns.domain=*" OR Web.uri_query="*dns.type=*" OR Web.uri_query="*dns.class=*" OR Web.url="*dns.server=*" OR Web.url="*dns.name=*" OR Web.url="*dns.domain=*") by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.http_method, Web.url, Web.uri_query, Web.status, Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime

Apache Camel DNS SSRF egress: app server (java) resolving via external / attacker DNS resolver AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the server-side effect of CVE-2026-48205: the Camel JVM issuing DNS queries (UDP/53) to a public resolver it should never talk to, because an attacker set dns.server to point SimpleResolver at an attacker-controlled DNS server. Internal app servers normally resolve only via internal forwarders, so outbound port-53 to a public IP from java is high-signal SSRF egress. Rationale: Targets the concrete SSRF payoff described in the advisory — SimpleResolver pointed at an attacker DNS server — by flagging java issuing UDP/53 to any non-private, non-corporate resolver, which is anomalous for a backend app that should use internal forwarders. Corporate public resolvers are allow-listed to cut noise. Pairs with UC1 (ingress) to confirm end-to-end exploitation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hcm8-x79p-wx2w • https://www.akamai.com/blog/security-research/march-apache-camel-vulnerability-detections-and-mitigations
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1046
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Camel route legitimately configured to query a public DNS resolver for a real DNS-integration use case
  • Java-based monitoring/APM agents performing external DNS lookups
  • App server placed in a segment without an internal DNS forwarder, resolving directly to public roots
  • Container images shipping with a hard-coded public resolver (e.g. 8.8.8.8) in resolv.conf overriding corporate DNS
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP !in ("8.8.8.8","8.8.4.4","1.1.1.1","1.0.0.1","9.9.9.9","208.67.222.222","208.67.220.220")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the DstIpAddr/RemoteIP the JVM queried — is it a known corporate/public resolver or an unfamiliar host? Correlate the same host+time window against UC1 web logs for an inbound dns.server=<that IP> request to confirm attacker control. 2) Contain: block egress UDP/53 from the app subnet to anything but internal forwarders, and repoint the Camel DNS server parameter to a trusted source in the route (or upgrade to 4.21.0/4.18.3/4.14.8). 3) Hunt: enumerate the dns.name/dns.domain values queried to see which internal hostnames the attacker probed, and review whether poisoned DNS responses drove any downstream connections from the host.

Apache Camel: camel-mongodb-gridfs producer allows GridFS operation override and NoSQL operator injection via unfiltered  gridfs.*  HTTP headers

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Apache Camel gridfs.* control-header injection inbound (CVE-2026-48204 exploit)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Apache Camel gridfs.* control-header injection inbound (CVE-2026-48204 exploit) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP requests carrying the unfiltered gridfs.* control headers (gridfs.operation / gridfs.objectid / gridfs.metadata / gridfs.chunksize / gridfs.fileid) that a camel-mongodb-gridfs producer will treat as an operation override or NoSQL-operator injection. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact literal header names that HttpHeaderFilterStrategy fails to strip and on the override operation values (remove/listAll/findOne) named in CVE-2026-48204. Rationale: Anchors on the five literal control-header names (gridfs.operation/objectid/metadata/chunksize/fileid) that GHSA-f7g3-2cg6-f5hj states bypass HttpHeaderFilterStrategy because they lack the camel/Camel prefix, plus the override operation tokens remove/listAll/findOne - all high-fidelity because no benign HTTP client sends these header names. Cross-checked cvedetails and the sibling Camel header-filter-bypass CVEs (CVE-2025-27636, CVE-2025-29891) which confirm the same unfiltered-header exploitation class. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f7g3-2cg6-f5hj • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-48204 • https://www.cvedetails.com/vulnerability-list/vendor_id-45/product_id-26278/Apache-Camel.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1499.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal QA / DAST scanners (Burp, ZAP, Nuclei) fuzzing the Camel HTTP endpoint with gridfs.* headers as part of authorized testing
  • A legitimate downstream integration that intentionally drives GridFS operations via the raw gridfs.* header names (pre-upgrade, not yet migrated to the CamelGridFs* constants)
  • Vulnerability-management scanners (Tenable, Qualys) probing for CVE-2026-48204 and logging benign detection traffic
  • WAF log noise where 'gridfs.' appears in an unrelated URL path segment rather than a control header
Suppression filter
| where isnull(OverrideOp) == false and OverrideOp in~ ("remove","listAll","findOne","delete")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request for the flagged source IP - confirm gridfs.operation is set to remove/listAll/findOne (not upload) and whether gridfs.metadata carries MongoDB operators ($where/$gt/$ne). Check the Camel app version against the fixed builds (4.14.8 / 4.18.3 / 4.21.0). 2) Contain: if the bridging consumer is unauthenticated and the version is vulnerable, block the source IP at the WAF and add a rule stripping gridfs.* request headers before the producer; set an explicit operation on the mongodb-gridfs endpoint. 3) Hunt: review GridFS/MongoDB audit logs for unexpected file deletions (remove), full-bucket listAll enumeration, or findOne reads from the app's service account in the same window; pivot on the source IP across all public-facing Camel routes.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceProduct has_any ("WAF","Application Gateway","F5","ModSecurity","Imperva") or isnotempty(RequestURL)
| where RequestURL has "gridfs." or Message has "gridfs." or RequestContext has "gridfs."
| extend Hay = strcat(tostring(RequestURL), " ", tostring(Message), " ", tostring(RequestContext))
| where Hay has_any ("gridfs.operation","gridfs.metadata","gridfs.objectid","gridfs.fileid","gridfs.chunksize")
| extend OverrideOp = extract(@"gridfs\.operation[=:\s""']+(\w+)", 1, Hay)
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Hits = count(), Ops = make_set(OverrideOp, 10), SampleReq = any(RequestURL) by SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestMethod, DeviceProduct
| order by LastSeen desc

When checking the URL isn’t enough: a Device Code Phishing attack via a Microsoft website

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-07-06 9 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant specification was designed to streamline authentication for Smart TVs, IoT devices, and printers. Today, threat actors are weaponizing it.

ATT&CKT1190 T1528 T1566 T1566.001

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Law-firm / order-confirmation lure delivering device-code phish via cacoo.com and allianceinvestigators.com · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Entra ID Device Authorization Grant (device code) authentication flow sign-in · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Post-device-code token abuse: mailbox / OneDrive / Teams access from a new IP after device-code sign-in · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Entra ID Device Authorization Grant (device code) authentication flow sign-in AIExploitation High
Hunts successful Entra ID sign-ins completed via the OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant (device code) flow — the exact mechanism abused in this campaign, where the attacker's server-side app fetches a user_code and the victim approves it (plus MFA) on Microsoft's legitimate page. Surfaces the users, client apps, source IPs and countries so an analyst can spot device-code auth on non-input-constrained principals (regular office users) that should never legitimately use it. Rationale: Anchors on the article's core mechanic: the OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant completed on login.microsoftonline.com. Sentinel's canonical AuthenticationProtocol=='deviceCode' column is used in the Sigma rule; the Defender/Sentinel bodies pivot on the in-schema AuthenticationProcessingDetails blob plus the Microsoft Authentication Broker client app because AuthenticationProtocol is not exposed in this tenant's Advanced-Hunting/Sentinel column set. Device code auth on regular knowledge-worker accounts is inherently anomalous. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/microsoft-device-code-phishing-attack/120350/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/v2-oauth2-device-code
ATT&CKT1528 T1566.002
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft Teams Rooms / smart-display or conference devices that legitimately enroll via device code
  • Admins running 'az login --use-device-code' or Azure PowerShell Connect-AzAccount -UseDeviceAuthentication
  • Intune / Autopilot device enrollment through the Microsoft Authentication Broker app
  • Kiosk or signage endpoints that lack a keyboard and use device code by design
  • Developers authenticating headless CI runners with device code
Suppression filter
| where AppDisplayName !in~ ("Microsoft Intune", "Microsoft Intune Enrollment", "Microsoft Teams Rooms")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm whether the AccountUpn is a device-constrained principal (Teams Room, kiosk, service). If it is a normal user, treat device-code sign-in as suspicious; check the source IP/country vs the user's baseline and whether MFA was satisfied. Step 2 (contain): Revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession / 'Revoke sessions' in Entra), force password reset, and block sign-in if the IP is foreign/unexpected. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on AccountObjectId across CloudAppEvents/OfficeActivity for MailItemsAccessed, Send, inbox-rule creation, and OneDrive downloads in the following 24h; review inbound EmailEvents to the user for the law-firm / order-confirmation lure and cacoo.com / allianceinvestigators.com URLs.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code" or AppDisplayName has "Microsoft Authentication Broker"
| where isnotempty(AccountUpn) and AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| summarize SignIns = count(), Apps = make_set(Application, 10), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), Countries = make_set(Country, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by AccountUpn, ClientAppUsed
| order by LastSeen desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code" or AppDisplayName == "Microsoft Authentication Broker"
| extend Loc = tostring(parse_json(tostring(LocationDetails)).countryOrRegion)
| summarize SignIns = count(), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), Countries = make_set(Loc, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, ClientAppUsed
| order by LastSeen desc

Law-firm / order-confirmation lure delivering device-code phish via cacoo.com and allianceinvestigators.com AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the inbound delivery stage of this campaign: emails styled as a law-firm notice (password-protected PDF) or a Portuguese order/quote confirmation whose links route through legitimate open-redirect infrastructure (cacoo.com) or the actor's legal-portal domain (allianceinvestigators.com) toward a device-code phishing page. Article-specific because it keys on the two confirmed IOC domains and the password-protected-PDF-with-link delivery pattern rather than generic phishing. Rationale: Uses the two article-confirmed IOC domains (cacoo.com used as an open redirect, allianceinvestigators.com as the mimicked legal portal) joined against inbound Safe-Links URL telemetry. AttachmentCount surfaces the password-protected-PDF variant. High-fidelity because these exact domains carrying inbound mail is rare and directly tied to the observed campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/microsoft-device-code-phishing-attack/120350/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1566.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Inbound mail from a genuine partner law firm that happens to attach password-protected PDFs
  • Marketing/newsletter senders embedding cacoo.com asset links
  • Internal users legitimately corresponding with allianceinvestigators.com if it is a real vendor in your supply chain
  • Safe Links rewriting a benign cacoo.com link inside a forwarded thread
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Open the flagged messages; confirm the lure (law-firm notice with password-protected PDF, or Portuguese order/quote confirmation) and follow the cacoo.com / allianceinvestigators.com URL chain to see whether it terminates on a device-code / copy-the-code page. Step 2 (contain): Soft-delete/quarantine matching messages tenant-wide (Threat Explorer > purge), block the sender and allianceinvestigators.com at the gateway, and add the redirect URL to the block list. Step 3 (hunt): For each recipient, check UrlClickEvents for a click-through and then pivot to UC1 (device-code sign-in) and UC3 (post-auth mailbox/OneDrive access) to determine which recipients actually authenticated.

| order by TimeGenerated desc
Post-device-code token abuse: mailbox / OneDrive / Teams access from a new IP after device-code sign-in AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates a successful device-code sign-in with follow-on cloud activity (MailItemsAccessed, mail Send, inbox-rule creation, OneDrive downloads) performed on the same account from a DIFFERENT source IP within 24h — the exact post-compromise behaviour described, where the attacker used the harvested access/refresh tokens to read and send mail, exfiltrate OneDrive files and access Teams. Article-specific because it is chained to the device-code auth event rather than a generic anomalous-access rule. Rationale: Chains the device-code auth event (article's credential-theft step) to the article's stated impact — reading/sending mail, OneDrive exfiltration, Teams access — and requires a source-IP change within 24h to strip legitimate device-code roaming. The IP-mismatch + short-window join is the noise reducer that separates attacker token replay from the user's own follow-on activity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/microsoft-device-code-phishing-attack/120350/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1114/
ATT&CKT1114 T1530 T1528
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User completes device-code auth on a kiosk then works from their laptop on a different NAT/egress IP
  • Corporate VPN or proxy rotation changing the egress IP between the auth and the activity
  • Mobile user roaming between cellular and Wi-Fi within the 24h window
  • Legitimate Teams Room / signage device auth followed by admin management from another IP
  • Outlook/OneDrive mobile client on a different carrier IP than the browser used to approve the code
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Compare AuthIP/AuthCountry with the activity IP/country; a foreign or hosting-provider (VPS) activity IP against a domestic auth is high-signal. Review which mailbox items were accessed, what was sent, and any newly created inbox rules. Step 2 (contain): Revoke the user's sessions and refresh tokens, disable any attacker-created inbox/forwarding rules, reset credentials, and block the activity IP. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate all messages Sent/forwarded during the window (BEC pivot), check OneDrive/SharePoint audit for bulk downloads, and sweep other users who received the same law-firm / order-confirmation lure for parallel device-code sign-ins.
let DeviceCodeAuth = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where ErrorCode == 0
    | where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code" or AppDisplayName has "Microsoft Authentication Broker"
    | project AuthTime = Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountUpn, AuthIP = IPAddress, AuthCountry = Country;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("MailItemsAccessed", "Send", "SendAs", "FileDownloaded", "FileSyncDownloaded", "New-InboxRule", "Set-InboxRule")
| join kind=inner DeviceCodeAuth on AccountObjectId
| where Timestamp between (AuthTime .. AuthTime + 24h)
| where isnotempty(IPAddress) and IPAddress != AuthIP
| project Timestamp, AuthTime, AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName, ActionType, Application, ActivityIP = IPAddress, ActivityCountry = CountryCode, AuthIP, AuthCountry, ObjectName
| order by Timestamp desc
let DeviceCodeAuth = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ResultType == 0
    | where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code" or AppDisplayName == "Microsoft Authentication Broker"
    | project AuthTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AuthIP = IPAddress;
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Operation in ("MailItemsAccessed", "Send", "SendAs", "FileDownloaded", "FileSyncDownloaded", "New-InboxRule", "Set-InboxRule")
| join kind=inner DeviceCodeAuth on $left.UserId == $right.UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated between (AuthTime .. AuthTime + 24h)
| where isnotempty(ClientIP) and ClientIP != AuthIP
| project TimeGenerated, AuthTime, UserId, Operation, OfficeWorkload, ClientIP, AuthIP, OfficeObjectId = OfficeId
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

phpBB CVE-2026-48611 auth bypass via login_link auth_provider=apache AIExploitation High
Hunts the exact CVE-2026-48611 exploit request: a single unauthenticated POST to ucp.php that triggers the login-link flow but forces the vulnerable 'apache' auth provider (auth_provider=apache) to skip the password check and log in as any user. The auth_provider=apache value inside a mode=login_link request is a near-unambiguous exploit signature that no legitimate default phpBB flow produces. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim PoC URL (/ucp.php?mode=login_link&auth_provider=apache&login_link_aikido=1); auth_provider=apache in a login_link request is the exact exploit primitive and has no benign default-config equivalent. Cross-checked against Pentest-Tools, IONIX, SentinelOne, phpBB.com advisory and public PoC repos. Cross-checked against: • https://pentest-tools.com/research/phpbb-authentication-bypass • https://www.ionix.io/threat-center/cve-2026-48611/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-48611/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/phpbb-forum-fixes-auth-bypass-bug-lurking-for-a-decade/ • https://www.phpbb.com/community/viewtopic.php?t=2672170
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanning (Nuclei has a public CVE-2026-48611 template) hitting the endpoint
  • Internal penetration-test / red-team validation of the patch
  • A phpBB instance legitimately fronted by an Apache .htpasswd proxy that genuinely uses the apache auth provider (rare, non-default)
  • Security researchers reproducing the PoC from the aikido.dev / GitHub repos against a lab instance
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("<scanner-ip-allowlist>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the target forum version — if < 3.3.17 (or 4.0.0-a2) it is exploitable; capture source IP, User-Agent, targeted login_username, and the HTTP status (302 = successful bypass). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, force-expire all active phpBB sessions (rotate the board's session salt / clear phpbb_sessions), and prioritise upgrade to 3.3.17 or apply the vendor workaround disabling the apache provider. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same source IP for follow-on /adm/index.php access, ACP user/permission changes, and private-message reads; review phpbb_log for admin actions after the exploit timestamp.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "ucp.php"
| where Url has "mode=login_link" and Url has "auth_provider=apache"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

phpBB CVE-2026-48611 post-exploit ACP access from exploiting IP AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates the CVE-2026-48611 exploit request (login_link + auth_provider=apache) with a subsequent hit to the phpBB Admin Control Panel (/adm/index.php) from the same source IP within one hour. This confirms the bypass yielded an admin session and the attacker is now operating the forum backend, separating real compromise from opportunistic scanning. Rationale: Uses the article's ACP path (/adm/index.php) plus the exact exploit query string, tied on source IP within a 1h window (3600s / 1h) — the exploit-then-admin sequence is what turns a scan into confirmed admin takeover. ACP path and admin impact confirmed against phpBB.com advisory and BleepingComputer. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/phpbb-forum-fixes-auth-bypass-bug-lurking-for-a-decade/ • https://www.phpbb.com/community/viewtopic.php?t=2672170 • https://pentest-tools.com/research/phpbb-authentication-bypass
ATT&CKT1078 T1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate admin who happens to share a NAT/egress IP with a scanner that probed the endpoint
  • Penetration test that both exploits and logs into ACP from the same host (expected TP but authorized)
  • WAF/proxy that rewrites source IP to a single upstream address, collapsing distinct users onto one src (tune to use X-Forwarded-For)
  • Load-balancer health checks hitting /adm/index.php returning 401/403 (filter on HttpStatusCode success)
Suppression filter
| where HttpStatusCode in (200, 302, 301)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm both events share the true client IP (check XFF if behind a proxy) and that the /adm access returned 200/302 rather than 401/403; identify which admin username was impersonated. 2) Contain: invalidate all sessions, disable/rotate the compromised admin account credentials, block the source IP, and enable maintenance mode until 3.3.17 is deployed. 3) Hunt: enumerate every ACP action from that session — new admin/mod accounts (acp_users, acp_groups), permission grants, board settings and email-config changes, and extension installs (potential webshell); diff phpbb_config and phpbb_users against a known-good backup.
let Exploit = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Url has "ucp.php" and Url has "mode=login_link" and Url has "auth_provider=apache"
    | project ExploitTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/adm/index.php"
| join kind=inner Exploit on SrcIpAddr
| where TimeGenerated between (ExploitTime .. ExploitTime + 1h)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, ExploitTime)
| project ExploitTime, AdminAccessTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpStatusCode, DelaySec
| order by ExploitTime desc
